network.overall_strategy: Construct L-Alanine from prebiotic simple molecules (CO2, NH3, H2, CH4, HCN, acetaldehyde) via diverse routes involving Strecker synthesis, reductive amination, transamination, and photochemical and mineral-catalyzed transformations. Branching from both hydrothermal and surface sources, converging on key intermediates like pyruvate, aminoacetonitrile, and imines. All pathways are justified by plausible geochemical and laboratory routes under early Earth conditions.

reactions.name: Reductive amination of pyruvate
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation of pyruvate and ammonia followed by FeS-catalyzed reduction to alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in prebiotic models (Muchowska et al., Nat. Ecol. Evol. 2017). FeS minerals catalyze reductive amination of pyruvate to alanine.

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of alanine
reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde reacts with ammonia and HCN to form aminoacetonitrile (AAN), precursor to alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker synthesis is robust for prebiotic amino acid formation using clays (Hill & Orgel, 2002).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of AAN to alanine
reactions.mechanism: Clay-catalyzed hydrolysis of AAN to yield L-alanine.
reactions.reasoning: AAN hydrolysis to amino acids is well established on mineral surfaces (Hill & Orgel, 2002; Saladino et al., 2001).

reactions.name: Pyruvate formation from acetaldehyde and CO2
reactions.mechanism: Sequential carboxylation and oxidation of acetaldehyde forms pyruvate.
reactions.reasoning: Metal sulfide catalysis for pyruvate synthesis is supported in hydrothermal analogs (Hafenbradl et al., 1995; Muchowska et al., 2017).

reactions.name: Pyruvate from acetic acid and formaldehyde
reactions.reasoning: Borate minerals stabilize intermediates permitting aldol condensation (Cairns-Smith et al., 1968).

reactions.name: UV photoreduction of HCN to acetaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Photoreduction and reduction by H2S convert HCN to acetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Photoreductive conversion reported under prebiotic surface conditions (Sutherland, 2016).

reactions.name: Transamination of pyruvate with methylamine
reactions.mechanism: Methylamine donates amino group to pyruvate, generating L-alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Transamination is plausible with FeS minerals (Heinen & Lauwers, 1996; speculative as prebiotic methylamine donor is less common).

reactions.name: Reductive amination of acetaldehyde to acetaldimine
reactions.mechanism: Imine of acetaldehyde with ammonia formed on clay surface.
reactions.reasoning: Imine formation on mineral surfaces is robust and demonstrated (Hill & Orgel, 2002).

reactions.name: Alpha-cyanation of acetaldimine to aminoacetonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Imine reacts with HCN yielding aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Alpha-cyanation pathway suggested by Strecker-related chemistry (Saladino et al., 2001).

reactions.name: Methylamine formation from formaldehyde and ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Condensation and reductive amination form methylamine.
reactions.reasoning: Prebiotic methylamine plausible by formose-type and reductive reactions (Cleaves, 2008).

reactions.name: Acetonitrile hydrolysis to acetic acid
reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydrolysis on clay mineral yields acetic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Acetonitrile hydrolysis to acetic acid is robust in aqueous clay environments (Cleaves, 2008).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde production from CH4 and CO2
reactions.mechanism: Partial oxidation of methane to formaldehyde via FeS and photochemically.
reactions.reasoning: Partial methane oxidation demonstrated in laboratory hydrothermal and surface settings (Ritson & Sutherland, 2012).

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal reductive amination
pathways.description: Formation of alanine via hydrothermal synthesis of acetaldehyde, pyruvate, and subsequent FeS-catalyzed reductive amination.

pathways.name: Surface Strecker route (classic)
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde undergoes Strecker reaction on clays to produce AAN, hydrolyzed to alanine.

pathways.name: Pyruvate via acetic acid aldol
pathways.description: Surface mineral-catalyzed aldol condensation between acetic acid and formaldehyde forms pyruvate, reductively aminated to alanine.

pathways.name: Pyruvate from methane, CO2 and surface cycling
pathways.description: Methane and CO2 yield formaldehyde and acetic acid, then pyruvate; converted to alanine.

pathways.name: Transamination route
pathways.description: Methylamine (from formaldehyde/ammonia) used to aminate pyruvate, yielding alanine and acetonitrile.

pathways.name: Aldimine-cyanation route
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde reacts with ammonia to form imine, which reacts with HCN to AAN, hydrolyzed to alanine.

pathways.name: Pyruvate creation via formaldehyde, then Strecker
pathways.description: Formaldehyde and acetic acid produce pyruvate, aminated directly to alanine.

pathways.name: Mixed Strecker/imine cycling
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde to imine, cyanation to AAN, hydrolysis to alanine—bypassing some classical intermediates.

pathways.name: Acetonitrile to acetic acid to pyruvate
pathways.description: Methylamine byproduct gives acetonitrile, hydrolyzed to acetic acid, converted to pyruvate and then alanine.

pathways.name: Primary hydrothermal photoredox route
pathways.description: HCN and H2S on the surface, under UV, photoreduce to acetaldehyde; proceeds through classic Strecker or imine intermediates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 combines hydrothermal transformation of acetaldehyde to pyruvate (rxn_004, unbalanced, missing water as a product) with reductive amination (rxn_001, unbalanced but balanceable with water as a byproduct). While the individual steps are commonly cited in prebiotic chemistry and plausible for the environments, the explicit absence of H2O in the reactions is a mass-balance issue. Target L-alanine is reached and the transitional logic is clear, but improper balancing lowers feasibility.
suggestions: Explicitly include H2O as a product in rxn_004 and rxn_001.
Review reaction equations for complete balancing to improve plausibility.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P2 follows the well-established Strecker synthesis and hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile to form L-alanine. Atom balance was unassessable due to formula parsing errors for 'AAN', but the reactions are plausibly prebiotic and typically feasible. Clarify AAN's identity formally and ensure balance for highest confidence.
suggestions: Specify AAN formula/structure for software parsing.
Verify stoichiometry to achieve atom conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pyruvate formation from acetic acid and formaldehyde (rxn_005) is problematic due to mass imbalance (missing H2 as product, or otherwise unconventional mechanism). Subsequent Strecker synthesis route is plausible given corrections to AAN, as above. Consider explicit balancing and mechanistic justification for the first step.
suggestions: Balance rxn_005 properly; consider if a redox partner is needed.
Clarify AAN in all relevant reactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Starts with balanced formaldehyde formation from methane/CO2 (rxn_012), but subsequent aldol (rxn_005) and Strecker reactions suffer from same balance and definition issues. Overall prebiotic plausibility is moderate; improves considerably with explicit balancing.
suggestions: Explicitly balance rxn_005; consider intermediates.
Clarify and verify all reactions involving AAN.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Transamination (rxn_007) is unbalanced with missing byproducts; methylamine synthesis (rxn_010) likewise. The pathway is conceptually coherent but hampered by atom conservation issues and an implausibly direct photoredox conversion for acetaldehyde (rxn_006). Major improvements needed in balancing.
suggestions: Insert missing byproducts, e.g., H2O, in all unbalanced reactions.
Provide mechanistic detail for rxn_006 or propose a more chemically plausible alternative.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aldimine formation (rxn_008) is only balanceable if H2O is specified as a product. Alpha-cyanation and hydrolysis are chemically sound (pending AAN clarification). A reasonable pathway with limited issues mostly related to explicit water production and AAN structure.
suggestions: Add H2O as a product in rxn_008.
Define the aminoacetonitrile node chemically in all reactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Utilizes a conceptually solid route from formaldehyde and ammonia to methylamine, then Strecker synthesis. All main reactions are plausible except for atom conservation issues with rxn_010 and AAN parsing. Good foundation—address these technical details for high confidence.
suggestions: Balance rxn_010 by including H2O as a byproduct.
Specify AAN structure or formula.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Follows mixed aldimine/cyanation and photoredox routes. Significant atom conservation issues in rxn_006 and requirement for explicit water in rxn_008. Better chemical definition and stoichiometry checking needed.
suggestions: Balance all reactions, especially rxn_008 and rxn_006.
Clarify AAN node.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Acetonitrile hydrolysis (rxn_011) is not atom balanced and mechanistically dubious under mild surface conditions. Downstream steps inherit the same balancing and AAN definition problems as in previous pathways.
suggestions: Re-express rxn_011 with proper stoichiometry.
Clarify all intermediate formulas.
Ensure atom and charge conservation in every reaction.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Primary hydrothermal photoredox route includes highly unbalanced and chemically questionable photoreduction of HCN to acetaldehyde (rxn_006), and needs balancing for reductive amination (rxn_001) and aldimine formation (rxn_008). Large mechanistic gaps.
suggestions: Review rxn_006 mechanism to ensure plausible atom flows.
Explicitly add missing byproducts in all steps.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network displays a sophisticated and diverse approach to prebiotic L-alanine synthesis, leveraging multiple plausible mechanisms and plausible environmental scenarios. However, widespread atom and charge conservation violations (missing byproducts, incomplete balancing, and undefined intermediates such as 'AAN') represent a major technical barrier. Many pathways are chemically plausible and literature-aligned in concept, but require explicit stoichiometric corrections and formal molecular definitions to be fully validated. Addressing reaction balancing and inputting definitive chemical identifiers for all intermediates will substantially improve network robustness. Best pathway (P6) is approved but still needs technical corrections; overall the network is promising but falls below the 0.9 threshold for universal approval.
